transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Um, well, I guess I'm here because... well, it's kind of embarrassing, honestly. I work as a secretary, an administrative assistant, so my whole job is supposed to be about keeping things organized and on track for other people. And usually, I can sort of manage to keep my head above water, but lately, it feels like my brain is just a sieve. 

What finally made me actually reach out and ask for help—which took me a while, because I kept thinking I just needed to buy a new planner or try harder—is that I just keep forgetting all these little things that I normally handle just fine. Like, I will completely forget to return phone calls, both at work and personal ones, or I will have a registration form filled out and sitting right there in my bag, and I just... never turn it in. Or even just simple everyday stuff, like I will tell myself I need to stop for an errand on the way home from work, maybe pick up something from the pharmacy or grab milk, and I will just drive straight home on autopilot and not even realize I forgot until I pull into my driveway. 

It is just so frustrating because I know I need to do these things, and I have every intention of doing them, but they just completely fall out of my head the second I look away. And it has been happening so much lately that it's driving me crazy, and I just felt like I couldn't keep brushing it off anymore, you know?
Looking back to your childhood and school years, did you struggle with attention and organization back then as well?

Oh, wow, yeah... honestly, yes. When I really sit down and think about it, it’s like this has been happening my entire life. My mom used to always say I’d lose my head if it wasn't attached to my neck, which, you know, was kind of a running joke in our family, but it was also really true. I mean, even way back in elementary school, I was always, always that kid. 

The one who completely forgot about permission slips until the morning of the field trip, or I'd actually remember to get it signed but then leave it sitting right there on the kitchen counter. And my backpack... oh my gosh, my backpack was basically a black hole. I would actually do my homework—I really would, I'd sit at the table and do it!—but then I'd shove it in my bag, and by the time I got to school, it was just lost in this sea of crumpled papers and old folders. I lost homework in my backpack all the time, and the teachers would look at me like I was just making up excuses. 

And don't even get me started on big assignments. Whenever we had a project, like a science fair thing or a book report, I just couldn't figure out how to get from the beginning to the end. I needed my mother—or sometimes my teacher, if we were working in class—to literally sit there and remind me step by step by step to finish it. Like, "Okay, first we cut the paper. Now we glue this part. Now write the title." If they didn't walk me through every single little step and keep me on track, I would just get completely overwhelmed or distracted and nothing would ever get done. It was so frustrating for my mom, bless her heart, and I always felt so bad about it, because I really was trying. I just... I don't know, my brain just didn't want to organize things the way everyone else's did, even back then. It's wild to think about how long it's been going on, really.
Do you often feel physically restless, fidgety, or have trouble sitting still?

Um, well, it's funny you ask that, because I wouldn't say I'm, like, running around the room or anything like that, you know? But... I do have this thing where I just can't seem to stay completely still, especially if I'm stuck in one place for a while. 

Like, back when I was in school, or even now if I have to sit through a long meeting or some sort of training seminar for work—which we have to do every quarter, and they are just agonizingly long, honestly, they could just be an email—I'll notice that I'm constantly, I don't know, just moving some part of my body. I'll be sitting there, and I really am trying to pay attention to the presenter, I really am, but my foot will just be bouncing up and down, up and down, under the table. Or I'll have a pen in my hand, and I'll just be clicking it over and over. Click, click, click. And I don't even realize I'm doing it until someone gives me a look, or I catch myself, and then I feel so embarrassed. 

And even if I stop the pen clicking, then I'm just shifting around in my chair. Like, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, leaning forward, leaning back. It's like my body just gets so uncomfortable if I try to hold it perfectly still for too long. It's not that I want to get up and leave—well, sometimes I do, because the meetings are boring—but it's more like this physical need to just let out some kind of energy, even when I'm really trying my hardest to just sit quietly and focus on what's being said. It's just this constant, subtle kind of squirming, I guess you could call it.
{"intent": "Assess the hyperactive symptom of feeling constantly 'on the go' or driven by a motor", "question": "Do you often feel like you are constantly 'on the go

Um, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I feel like I'm driven by a motor or anything like that. It's actually kind of the opposite sometimes, if I'm being perfectly honest. I see people who are just constantly go, go, go, you know? Like my sister-in-law, she's always doing something, volunteering for the PTA, running marathons, remodeling her kitchen on the weekends, and I just look at her and think, "Where do you even find the energy for all of that?" 

Because for me, it's not like I have this endless supply of physical energy pushing me to always be doing something. Like I said before, I do get fidgety, and I definitely have trouble just sitting completely still without my foot tapping or shifting around, but it's not like I feel this intense need to be running around or constantly busy. If anything, by the time I get home from work, after trying to keep track of everyone else's schedules and emails all day, I just feel completely drained. 

I'll walk through the door, and all I want to do is just sit on the couch and stare at the wall for a little bit, just to let my brain kind of decompress, you know? It's more of a mental exhaustion than a physical one, but it definitely doesn't leave me feeling like I need to be constantly on the move. So, yeah, I guess I wouldn't really describe myself as being 'on the go' all the time. It's more like my brain is on the go, just spinning and spinning, but my body is perfectly fine just staying put. If I could just get my brain to sit as still as my body wants to sometimes, I think I'd be in much better shape! But yeah, no, no motor here, just a lot of mental noise, I guess you could say.
Do you often find yourself talking excessively, or feel like it is hard to stop once you get started?

Um, no, I wouldn't say so. Actually, it's kind of funny because at work—I'm an administrative assistant, so I'm sitting right there at the front desk a lot of the time—I have to talk to people literally all day long. You know, answering the phones, greeting the clients when they come in for meetings, coordinating with the delivery guys who bring our office supplies... it's just a lot of interacting. But I'm definitely way more of a listener. I mean, I have to be, just to make sure I get all the messages written down correctly, otherwise things just completely fall through the cracks. 

But even outside of work, I never really feel that urge to just take over a conversation or talk someone's ear off. Like, my boss will stand by my desk and just go on and on and on about his weekend or his golf swing or his kids, and I just sit there nodding and saying "oh, wow" and "uh-huh." I never feel like I'm the one who can't stop talking. If anything, I'm usually the one standing there trying to figure out how to politely wrap things up and end the conversation so I can get back to what I was doing. Because, like I said before, if I don't write a note down right that exact second, the thought is just gone. 

I mean, I do chat with my friends, obviously. If we go out for lunch or something, we catch up, but I never feel like I'm dominating the table or that the words are just spilling out of me and I can't put a lid on it. In big groups, I'm actually pretty quiet. I mostly just kind of fade into the background and let everyone else carry the conversation. My husband actually jokes that getting a full story out of me after work is like pulling teeth sometimes, because I'll just give him the bare minimum unless we're talking about something really, really specific. So, um, yeah, I definitely wouldn't call myself an excessive talker at all. I'm perfectly happy just being quiet and letting other people do the talking.
Do you have a lot of trouble waiting your turn, such as waiting in lines or waiting for your turn in group situations?

Um, waiting my turn? No, I wouldn't say I have a lot of trouble with that. I mean, nobody likes waiting in lines, right? Like, if I go to the grocery store on a Sunday afternoon and there are only two registers open and the lines are stretching all the way down the aisles into the dairy section, I'm definitely not thrilled about it. But I don't feel like I'm going to jump out of my skin or anything. I just kind of stand there and wait like everybody else. 

I actually kind of use that time to zone out a little bit. Like, I'll just be staring at the magazines on the rack or looking at the candy bars, and my mind will just wander off to what I need to make for dinner or if I remembered to run the dishwasher before I left the house. Sometimes I'll just pull out my phone and scroll through things, but it's not because I'm so impatient that I can't handle waiting. It's just something to do while I'm standing there. 

And in group situations, like at work, I'm actually really good at waiting my turn. Like I was saying before, I'm much more of a listener anyway. So if we're having a staff meeting and everyone is talking over each other to give their updates, I'm perfectly fine just sitting back and waiting until there's a natural lull in the conversation to jump in. Or honestly, sometimes I just wait until someone specifically asks me a question. I never feel this burning need to interrupt people or push my way to the front of the line. 

I think part of it is because I'm so used to managing other people's schedules and making sure everyone else is where they need to be. Like, if I have three people waiting in the lobby to see different people in the office, I have to be the one who stays calm and just handles them one at a time. I can't get antsy about it, or it just makes them antsy, you know? So, yeah, I'd say waiting is definitely not one of my big issues. I'm pretty patient when it comes to that sort of thing. I might be completely checked out mentally while I'm waiting, but physically, I'm just hanging out, waiting my turn.
